catalog_quote: p. 469: "(33) Asymmetrical reflexes of *a…i and *a…u in Dorig: POC *ʀapiʀapi ‘evening’ > *raβiraβi > raːβrɪβ; POC *kanikani ‘eat’ > ɣaːnɣɪn; °sarusaru (#134) ‘wear’ > saːrsɪr; °m[w]ab[w]usaɣi (#104) ‘breathe; take rest’ > maːbsɪɣ. Interestingly, although Dorig is otherwise a well-behaved oxytone language (e.g., [marˈmar] ‘hard’), the presence of a long /aː/ word-internally tends to attract word stress: [ˈraːβrɪβ]." — p. 468: "the long vowel /aː/ of Dorig normally only occurs once within the word." — p. 451 (areal, all 17 Torres-Banks languages incl. Dorig): "The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77). Exactly the same evolution is attested in modern French: due to the progressive loss of all etymological posttonic vowels, French has become a perfectly oxytone language."

new_statements.quote: In the case of northern Vanuatu languages, there is every likelihood that the final consonants of POc forms had been lost at some stage (e.g., ‘ten’ *saŋapuluq > *saŋapulu); this resulted in vowel-final lexemes that systematically received primary stress on their penultimate syllable, and secondary stress every second syllable leftward (e.g., *saŋapulu). [...] The loss of word-final posttonic vowels explains why, in essentially all the languages of the area, words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77). Exactly the same evolution is attested in modern French: due to the progressive loss of all etymological posttonic vowels, French has become a perfectly oxytone language.

The key sentence 'in essentially all the languages of the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the modern Torres-Banks languages of the author's 17-language corpus (Dorig = DRG among them), word stress falls systematically on the final syllable; this is the historical outcome of penultimate proto-stress followed by loss of post-tonic vowels.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for the modern languages; for the proto-language, secondary stress every second syllable leftward of the penultimate primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged as 'essentially all the languages of the area' without naming the exceptions (Mota, which kept many final vowels, is the likely outlier; Dorig underwent full vowel reduction). No Dorig-specific exceptions given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('words are now systematically stressed on their final.. syllable'); statement is areal/comparative, made by the only linguist with first-hand Dorig field data, not in a Dorig-specific description. François's own transcription of the language name, Dōrig [ⁿdʊˈriɰ], shows final stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (François 2005: 451) is an areal generalisation over the author's 17-language Torres-Banks corpus ('essentially all the languages of the area'), in which Dorig [DRG, weta1242] is explicitly one of the 17 (own fieldwork, Gaua 2003); it is not a Dorig-specific sentence. Consistent with it, François transcribes the village/language name Dōrig as [ⁿdʊˈriɰ] with final stress (Pangloss corpus page; Wikipedia). 'Wetamut' is the older literature name for the same language (not recognised by speakers).

readall_conflicts: Lynch 2000 says nothing about Dorig, so there is no direct conflict with the catalog. The one indirect disagreement is areal: Lynch 2000:59 and :77 classify Mwotlap (the only Banks-Islands language he cites, on Crowley's TOL sketch) as a regular penultimate-syllable stress language even in consonant-final words ('ne-vet, 'kemem, 'na-yhow), whereas François 2005:451 (already in existing_statements, and explicitly marked "contra Lynch 2000:77") states that in essentially all northern Vanuatu languages, Dorig included, stress is now on the final syllable, and François 2005:469 calls Dorig "a well-behaved oxytone language" with word-internal long /aː/ attracting stress. Lynch's statement is second-hand and pre-dates any Dorig data; François's is first-hand, so the catalog's final-stress reading stands. Lynch's remark (p. 77) that the Southern Vanuatu-style shift to penultimate stress "may explain similar developments in languages like Mwotlap" is a diachronic conjecture, not a description of Dorig.
